query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting Al for Si or Mn in CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys reduces interfacial misfit strain and atomic diffusion rates at the metal/oxide boundary above 900 °C, thereby promoting a coherent, slow-growing protective oxide scale rather than one that cracks and spalls.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in either single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states with X = Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples to a controlled oxidative/corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C while performing real-time, in situ high-temperature oxidation measurements (e.g., environmental TEM and atom probe tomography).
generation.conditions: High-temperature (>900 °C) exposure in an oxidative or corrosive environment, with tests conducted under identical thermal and atmospheric conditions to allow a comparative assessment of oxide formation, growth kinetics, and scale coherence.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial misfit strain and element-dependent atomic diffusion at the metal/oxide interface.
generation.mechanism: The choice of X element modulates the atomic diffusion rate and interfacial stress at the metal/oxide boundary. In Al-containing alloys, lower diffusion rates and reduced misfit strain support the formation of a coherent, slow-growing protective oxide. In contrast, Si or Mn promotes higher interfacial strain and faster oxide growth that leads to crack initiation and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions, the Al-containing CrFeCoNiAl alloy will develop a thin, coherent, and slowly growing oxide scale with minimal cracking, whereas the Si- and Mn-containing alloys will show signs of rapid oxide buildup, increased interfacial strain, and subsequent crack formation and spallation.
generation.baseline: The Si- or Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys (or previously studied baselines such as CrMoTiAlY in similar conditions) serve as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in single- or multiphase states at service-relevant temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: While advanced in situ characterization can observe interface strain and diffusion effects, quantitative differences among the X elements (Al vs. Si vs. Mn) and the role of multiphase microstructures require further detailed measurement and may introduce variability outside the controlled conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX samples with X = Al, Si, and Mn. Subject each sample to an identical oxidative/corrosive environment at temperatures above 900 °C while directly monitoring oxide layer growth, interfacial coherence, and residual stress evolution using in situ environmental TEM and atom probe tomography over a defined time period.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate
Onset and extent of interfacial cracking or spallation
Diffusion profiles of X elements and other metallic constituents at the metal/oxide interface
Residual stress levels at the oxide/metal boundary
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial strain, slower oxide growth, and fewer or delayed cracking events compared to the Si- or Mn-containing alloys, or if all alloys exhibit similar oxide degradation behavior regardless of the X element, the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on the considered alloy systems (CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY) used empirical, long‐term high temperature oxidation tests to record which compositions developed unstable, spalling oxides, without pinpointing the physical causes of failure. Then, studies on refractory high‐entropy alloys, such as the work on CrTaO4‐based oxides, demonstrated that specific oxide phases could form protective, slow‐growing scales, but the reasoning behind why only certain compositions yield these stable layers remained unresolved. Most recently, advanced in‐situ characterization methods (atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption techniques) have been applied to decouple atomic size effects and redox potential influences on speciated oxide growth, offering mechanistic insight into oxidation processes. However, a systematic, controlled study directly comparing the effects of different X elements (Si, Mn, or Al) on the formation, coherence, and long‐term stability of the protective oxide layer above 900 °C is still missing.
decision.unsolved: The outstanding challenge is to determine how the substitution of the X element (Si, Mn, or Al) in CrFeCoNiX alloys controls the atomic diffusion and interfacial strain at the metal/oxide boundary that, in turn, governs whether a coherent, slow-growing, and protective oxide layer forms rather than one that cracks and spalls under high temperature. This precise mechanistic connection, including the role of potential misfit strain and elemental redox behavior, has not yet been directly quantified.
decision.lever: Conduct controlled, real-time high-temperature oxidation experiments on CrFeCoNiX alloys (with systematic variation of X = Si, Mn, or Al) using techniques such as environmental TEM and atom probe tomography. Key measurements would include oxide growth kinetics, interface coherence, and residual stress evolution at temperatures above 900 °C under oxidative/corrosive atmospheres.
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend of employing advanced, in-situ characterization methods to resolve atomic-scale mechanisms observed in previous studies. By isolating the effects of the X element in a controlled variable experiment, researchers can test whether modulating atomic diffusion and interfacial strain indeed governs the formation and integrity of the protective oxide layer, which is the central unresolved cue from earlier work.
